Power and youth. YOUTH are highly innovative in expressing their anger. Meanwhile, ruling elites struggle to understand that the existing power structure can no longer meet the aspirations of the young. The context of this statement is neither the events in Delhi, where the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) succeeded in achieving its demands , nor the violent protests in Azad Jammu and Kashmir , nor the recent provocative statement by the federal interior minister about the state system . Rather, the reference is to a silent protest by the youth of Khuzdar in Balochistan, in which they succeeded in having their demand met. Is it not a unique event in Pakistan when the demands of the youth are met? What was the youth’s demand? The reopening of a local library, where students study and prepare for their civil service examinations. The library was closed by the local bureaucracy, quite likely with the consent of superior institutions, which see books and libraries as sources of dissent. One cannot spare the bureaucracy either, which has a narrow vision and has been taught to rule like colonial masters. There is a high probability that in Khuzdar, too, they would have seen the youth’s inclination towards books and literature as a potential threat to security. It is ironic that most students, including many female students, were using the library as a safe and peaceful space to prepare for their exams. Most of them aspired to become bureaucrats, but the bureaucracy itself had shut down the library and closed the door to their future. Whatever factors were involved in the library’s shutdown, the youth adopted a unique and peaceful way to protest. They held a sit-in outside the library and converted the footpaths and adjoining street into an open-air study space. They did not raise any slogans or attempt to confront the police or the local administration; they simply continued sitting silently and studying. Finally, the Balochistan chief minister intervened, and the library doors opened again. This peaceful protest happened in a conflict-torn province where an insurgency is at its peak. The state has cracked down on violent actors. Sadly, those who participate in peaceful political and civil rights movements are also targeted. The district of Khuzdar has its own complex local, tribal and political context, and sardars, good or bad, have made the local people’s lives miserable. Yet the youth found a way to register their protest. The youth are not politically blind; they see how the system works and how it is manoeuvred. The protests by the youth in Khuzdar and by the CJP in India were related to education and inspired by the idea of getting a fair chance in life. Power structures have lost sight of the fact that equal opportunities and a fair system are essential for the youth. The youth are not politically blind; they see how the system works and how it is manoeuvred. Whether it is referred to as Gen Z or Alpha-Z, this is a different generation with a different worldview. A dominant trend, especially among the more privileged youth of this generation, is to try out new modes of production and expand their class influence. Their forefathers accumulated leverage for their protection through wealth and relationships within the power structure. Less privileged youth are becoming less interested in civil services and industries and more interested in the corporate and financial sectors. Certainly, the majority still belong to the middle- and lower-income groups, and they try every avenue they believe can empower them. They know that power is the only pathway to economic prosperity. Civil services and public-sector jobs of any sort are their shortcuts to finding a way out. When someone tries to block the path to their dreams, they resist and protest. The older generations respond to the new generation in the conventional way, claiming that the new generation knows nothing. Where the youth have brought about political change, as in Nepal and Bangladesh, senior figures in the system dislike them and see their worldview as flawed. A crisis is unfolding in Pakistan, particularly for the country’s youth. A draconian shift is taking place in the world of politics, where the older generation of politicians is transferring its legacy, power, and values to the next generation — not through legitimate constitutional and political means, but through shady deals with the most powerful. This process is occurring in every party, and the transition is frightening because those to whom power is being transferred have very little connection with political processes. They believe they are chosen to rule and can do anything to retain power. The youth of the country, then, has nothing to be proud of or to be inspired by in the existing political order. This piece is not meant to predict any Gen Z-style uprising in Pakistan, but to point out that the political structure has become so tarnished and corrupt that it cannot sustain the burden of the economy, create new economic engines, or effectively utilise the existing sources of wealth. The bureaucratic structure is incapable of running governance and is becoming increasingly ruthless. A sense of deprivation is a common thread among young people from the middle- and lower-income classes. Those in power are unwilling to review their practices; instead, they believe in an authoritarian, hegemonic style of controlling the system, in which subjects are expected to behave and follow whatever those in power dictate. The concept of citizenship was eroded long ago, and those who are powerless are treated merely as subjects. If they protest and their demands are fulfilled, they must consider themselves lucky, be thankful to the powerful, and forget that their success has anything to do with their ability to express themselves differently. The writer is a security analyst. Published in Dawn, August 2nd, 2026

Rethinking the auto policy. PAKISTAN’S automobile industry captures the country’s industrial policy dilemma well. As the government considers lower tariffs, manufacturers warn of plant closures, job losses and wasted investment. Critics argue that, despite more than 40 years of protection, consumers until recently faced high prices and limited choice, while exports remained negligible. Both sides have a point. But the debate is framed wrongly. The question is: can the country’s auto industry build capabilities that can compete in regional and global value chains? One principle should guide policy. Except in strategically important sectors, any industry seeking protection must offer consumers better value and move towards international competitiveness. Protection should be a runway, not a refuge. The auto industry deserves credit. It has built assemblers and component suppliers, developed engineering skills, invested in vendors and created skilled jobs despite expensive energy, costly finance, policy uncertainty, cumbersome regulation and weak logistics. But the main goals — saving foreign exchange through localisation and creating large-scale employment — were flawed from the start. Can Pakistan’s auto industry build capabilities that can compete in regional and global value chains? The first misconception was localisation. Auto policy assumed that making more components at home would ease pressure on the external account. That ignored how modern vehicles are made. Engines, transmissions, fuel injection systems, electronic controls and software carry much of a vehicle’s value. Producing them competitively requires deep upstream capacity in automotive-grade steel, petrochemicals, specialised alloys, precision engineering and electronics. Pakistan never built those foundations at scale, so localisation became a numerical target rather than a measure of real competitiveness. Localisation numbers are also misleading. They count components assembled domestically, not domestic value added. Seats, batteries, tyres, wiring harnesses, glass, plastic mouldings and metal stampings may be made locally, but many depend on imported inputs and moulds and use energy generated from imported fuels. A 50 to 60 percent localisation rate can therefore produce far smaller foreign exchange savings than advertised. Better metrics would track net domestic value addition, foreign exchange displacement and exports of locally manufactured components. The second misconception was jobs. Automobile manufacturing is capital-intensive. It relies heavily on automation because quality and precision leave little room for manual shortcuts. Pakistan’s largest assembler employs fewer than 2,500 people directly, and the three largest together less than 6,000. Suppliers add jobs, but the direct workforce remains small relative to the protection received. Dealerships, distribution and repair facilities would exist even if vehicles were imported fully built. The third misconception was scale. Competitive automobile manufacturing depends on large volumes that spread fixed costs across millions of vehicles. Pakistan’s market, at fewer than 300,000 vehicles a year, is too small to support that model on its own. Policy made matters worse by treating motor vehicles as luxury goods and taxing demand down. One arm of government protected local assembly while another choked the scale needed to make it efficient. The domestic consumer paid for both. None of this negates the industry’s achievements. It shows that policy was flawed and measured success against goals the industry’s structure made difficult, and at times impossible, to meet. Technology has now made the old debate even less useful. The global industry is moving from internal combustion engines to hybrids and EVs, changing where value is created. EVs eliminate or simplify many components around which Pakistan’s localisation strategy has traditionally been built. Engines, multi-speed gearboxes, exhaust systems, catalytic converters and fuel injection technologies become less important. Value shifts instead to batteries, electric motors, power electronics, battery management systems, semiconductors, sensors and software. Pakistan must stop designing industrial policy around yesterday’s technologies. Hybrids are the practical bridge: they cut fuel use and emissions without depending on charging infrastructure or an electricity network not yet ready for mass EV adoption. The policy goal should no longer be higher localisation percentages. It should be higher domestic value addition, exports, lower environmental impact and deeper technological capability. Incentives should favour battery assembly, electric motors, power electronics, charging equipment, automotive software, precision engineering and advanced manufacturing. Pakistan’s IT sector can support connected vehicles, while commercially viable minerals should feed domestic battery material and mobility supply chains rather than leave the country with minimal processing. Pakistan should position itself as a base for export-oriented investment, especially for Chinese EV producers looking to diversify production and reach regional markets. This will require predictable policy, competitive energy, efficient logistics, easier access to imported inputs and trade agreements that open real market access. Morocco shows what scale and access can achieve — it exports about 500,000 of the 600,000 vehicles it produces to the EU. Successful automotive producers offer clear lessons. Japan, South Korea, China and Thailand supported their auto industries, but protection was temporary, conditional and tied to exports, productivity, technology transfer and upgrading. India built its auto sector behind restrictions on consumer choice, while Asean and Mercosur countries used regional production networks to achieve scale. Pakistan should draw from these experiences, but it cannot simply replicate them as its domestic market is too small, regional integration is weak and the technology frontier has moved on. Tariffs in Pakistan should fall through a transparent, predictable schedule that gives firms time to adjust but no excuse to stand still. Government must lower economy-wide costs through energy, logistics and tax reform, while linking any remaining incentives to exports, domestic value addition, engineering depth and high-value hybrid and EV technologies — not production volumes or headline localisation rates. The real choice is not protection or liberalisation. It is whether Pakistan keeps measuring success by yesterday’s metrics or prepares for tomorrow’s automotive industry. The next auto policy should reward value addition, exports, innovation and technological transformation, and not permanence behind tariff walls. That would serve manufacturers, consumers and competitiveness far better than another decade of sterile debate. The writer is a former CEO of Unilever Pakistan and of the Pakistan Business Council. Trump says US 'locked and loaded' but will hold off on fresh Iran attack in hope of quick deal. United States President Donald Trump said late on Saturday he would hold off on a fresh attack on Iran as long as a deal could be reached quickly to halt Iran’s nuclear ambitions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iran and “other Middle Eastern Countries” asked for a time to complete a deal that would lead to “the Immediate, Complete and Total” reopening of the Strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. “Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL.” Israel “joins me in this commitment,” Trump wrote. Israel did not immediately make a public statement on the issue. Iran warned the US this weekend against any adventurous action and said it would retaliate decisively if American forces followed through on Trump’s threats of fresh attacks on Iranian targets. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchis comments in separate phone calls on Saturday with senior Turkish, Pakistani and Saudi officials came just hours after Kuwait’s army said it destroyed hostile drones launched by Iran against several vital facilities. Speaking to Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Araqchi said Iran would respond decisively to any “aggression” and discussed the consequences of destabilising actions” by the US, as well as prospects for heightened regional insecurity, according to Araqchi’s Telegram account. Araqchi later told Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan that any attacks by the US and Israel or participation by regional countries in such actions would be met with a proportionate response. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke to Trump on Saturday and “expressed concern and asked for clarity” about Us plans for Iran, a US official told Axios . The Saudi crown prince spoke to Trump, a White House official told Reuters , but did not provide details. Nournews , a media outlet affiliated with Iran’s top security body, said on Saturday that US attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure would prompt Iranian strikes on oil fields in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, as well as the gas fields of Qatar and Israel, saying, “all will be burned to ashes”. At a cabinet meeting on Friday at the Camp David retreat, Trump said he believed US negotiators, including his son-in-law Jared Kushner, special envoy Steve Witkoff and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, could still reach a deal with Iran. But Trump also said he was losing faith in the Iranians, saying, “They break their word so often” a claim Tehran has frequently levelled at Washington and said he would be “hitting them”. Strait of Hormuz Oil prices have stayed high since US and Israeli forces started the war with strikes on Iran on February 28. Trump has argued that his stated goal of keeping Iran from gaining nuclear weapons justifies higher fuel costs in the near term, but the economic pain has put political pressure on him to find a way to end the war. Benchmark Brent crude futures rose 24 per cent in July, and analysts polled by Reuters expect prices to rise further this year. The risk of Iranian attacks has deterred most shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, an important conduit for global energy supplies, since the start of the conflict, sending shockwaves through the world economy. A government facility in northern Kuwait and civilian property belonging to a company on Bubiyan Island were hit on Saturday, with falling shrapnel causing material damage but no casualties, the Kuwaiti army said. Adding to the energy industry’s concerns, the Houthis in Yemen recently began threatening the Bab el-Mandeb, the strait at the other end of the Red Sea from the Suez Canal, another export route for Saudi crude. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Saturday it had received reports of two maritime incidents off Oman, including one in which a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile that damaged the engine room. In the other incident, the master of a tanker reported seeing a large splash and an explosion close to the vessel, though no damage was reported.

SMOKERS’ CORNER: BEYOND THE ‘GEN-Z REVOLUTION’ LABEL. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will not fall, but he clearly wears a shell-shocked expression these days, as widespread anti-Modi protests by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) appear to have unnerved him. The CJP operates outside conventional politics as a movement driven primarily by young Indians. Naturally, following regional trends, where commentators labelled recent anti-government uprisings in Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh as Gen-Z uprisings, the Indian movement is receiving the same description. In truth, this term is intellectually lazy. Global student protests against governments in the late 1960s were never termed Boomer uprisings, nor were violent anti-corporate demonstrations in the 1990s described as Gen-X uprisings. Revolutions in places such as Ukraine and erstwhile Czechoslovakia received colour-coded names such as the Orange Revolution, Velvet Revolution etc. Western media delights in such terminology. This silly practice ultimately collapsed alongside the disastrous unravelling of the so-called Arab Spring , which no one labelled a Millennial uprising. How did the term ‘Gen Z revolution’ originate? Back in 2017, as the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement peaked in the United States, Pepsi attempted to capitalise on the momentum. A television commercial featured a well-known female model walking into a fictionalised BLM protest carrying a can of Pepsi, which she offered as a peace offering to the cops and the young protesters. From Nepal and Sri Lanka to Bangladesh and India, youth-led protests have become a regional phenomenon. But reducing them to generational branding obscures the political and economic forces driving them What the brand’s marketing team believed would be a stroke of corporate co-optation badly misfired . Young Americans took to social media to lambast Pepsi for trivialising the movement. The backlash proved so intense that Pepsi was forced to issue a public apology. Until 2017, most corporate brands remained oblivious to the fact that Millennials had already entered the workforce and were no longer the sole dominant youth demographic. A new generation was steadily replacing them: Generation-Z. Shaped by distinct circumstances, this cohort embraced markedly different values. Now every youth uproar is lazily labelled as a ‘Gen-Z uprising.’ Nepal witnessed youth-led uprisings driven by frustration with government corruption, nepotism and restrictions on civil liberties. Bangladesh experienced student protests initially sparked by anger over discriminatory civil service job quotas, which quickly broadened into a wider rebellion against authoritarian rule and youth unemployment. Sri Lanka’s upheaval was ignited by a severe economic crisis featuring shortages of fuel, food and medicine, alongside hyperinflation. India’s youth movement emerged in response to economic anxieties surrounding unemployment, and perceived threats to democratic norms. But here are three interesting bits about the uprising in India which haven’t been discussed in much detail. Political analysis and sociological studies by organisations such as Centre for the Study of Developing Societies-Lokniti (CSDS-Lokniti) show that Modi has historically enjoyed strong backing from young middle-class Indians. Therefore, the current youth protests in India against governance issues such as unemployment or exam irregularities mostly involve individuals or households that previously supported him, reflecting a move from optimistic aspiration to economic disillusionment. As the Pakistani political commentator Najam Sethi observed, this change implies that a significant segment of young Modi supporters is now open to engagement by anti-Modi parties. Secondly, the movement is horizontal, lacking a disciplined party structure and a central leader. This was also the case in Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. Horizontal movements fail to achieve any significant structural transformation. A despised individual may fall, but the underlying apparatus remains intact. This dynamic was also visible in the Arab Spring. However, horizontal movements have the potential to inadvertently unleash grave dangers as well. Consider a rubber-band. Stretched to its utmost limit, it either snaps back to its original shape upon release or, if pulled too far, breaks entirely. The 2018 youth uprising in Sudan successfully ousted a hated dictator, but the rubber-band broke rather than returning to its previous form. The country plunged into a brutal civil war that persists today. Historically, enduring revolutions capable of delivering structural change have required an organised outfit and a strong central leadership. They have a consensual hierarchy. Horizontal uprisings, on the other hand, generally achieve little beyond removing a head of state or government while preserving the ruling order, or risk fracturing the state into civil conflict. In India, the removal of Narendra Modi is not yet on the horizon, nor is there any likelihood of severe civil strife. What is visible, however, is an outpouring of frustration, directed at a once-revered figure by a youth demographic that includes many who previously idolised him and bought into his promises of economic miracles. This discontent was further compounded when he faltered in the 2025 conflict against arch-rival Pakistan. And this is important because it leads directly into the third interesting bit. Over the past few years, youth have risen up in almost every South Asian country, including Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh, the Maldives to a certain extent, and now India. Pakistan, however, has experienced nothing of the sort on a national scale. While protests have occurred, they remain ethnically localised, such as the canal protests exclusive to Sindh or the missing persons demonstrations confined to Balochistan. One might posit that the May 9, 2023 protests led by the Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) served as the nation’s Gen-Z uprising moment, but this characterisation misses the mark. The youth movements elsewhere in the region were organically driven by socio-economic grievances, whereas the May 9 mobilisation was a top-down, party-engineered response, cantered entirely around the personality and arrest of a single political leader, Imran Khan. Rather than representing an autonomous youth uprising confronting institutional failure, it was a partisan reaction executed by loyal party cadres defending a specific political figure, lacking the broad, non-partisan defiance that defines contemporary youth uprisings across the region. It signified little more than the uncritical adoration of a single leader. It is striking that major youth uprisings have erupted across South Asian nations that have historically experienced significant Indian economic and political influence, often leaving them feeling pressured to align with New Delhi’s regional preferences. This dynamic helps explain why anti-establishment sentiment in those countries frequently carried an explicit anti-India undertone. Pakistan stood apart as the sole nation in the region with a strictly anti-India posture. This altered its political ecosystem. While other South Asian states faced domestic movements targeting leadership perceived as compliant with India, Pakistan’s national narrative has long been anchored in hostility toward India. Therefore, ever since the late 1960s, anti-establishment anger in Pakistan tends to be channelled through ethnic-nationalist and partisan paradigms rather than through a broad, organic youth uprising. Asif reacts to Naqvi's call for governance reset, urges him to begin with his own ministry. Reacting to Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s call for an overhaul of the country’s governance structure, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has advised him to initiate the change by implementing the National Action Plan (NAP) and with his own ministry. Speaking at the Pakistan Economic Summit on Thursday, Naqvi had said the governance system in the country had “collapsed” and argued that the country needed new administrative units, or provinces, to improve service delivery, accountability and access to justice. He had also said new leadership was needed in the country and argued that the youth wanted justice, merit and jobs rather than stipends and laptops. A day later, the military’s spokesperson also urged political parties to consider an administrative reset for improving governance, arg­uing that the country’s security and stability depe­nded on adapting its governance structure to the requirements of modern times and a growing population. Speaking at a news conference, Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said governance had long been identified by the military as a prerequisite for nat­ional security. Further recalling the NAP adopted after the 2014 Army Public School attack, he said its 14-point agenda, unanimously endor­sed by political parties, had also rested on effective governance. On Saturday, Asif reacted to Naqvi’s suggestion in an X post, in which he also mentioned the DG ISPR’s remarks. “Mohsin Naqvi’s sahib expressed his views on the dire state of the system. I more or less personally agree with these views,” he said, calling the interior minister a “powerhouse”. Asif added that as a political worker, he too strongly felt the process of the system’s evolution had been “held captive to factional and personal interests for decades, and it needs to be freed”. He said he had a few requests in this regard, adding: “If the system has to be strengthened and a fundamental change has to be brought about, its forum is Parliament, of which Naqvi sahib is a member. Or this matter could be discussed in the cabinet. “This way, these institutions and the system would strengthen, and the change would be brought about through a constitutional process.” Asif went on to point out Naqvi was also a member of the cabinet, further claiming that he rarely attended parliamentary and cabinet sessions. He said: “In my opinion, [treating] these institutions as irrelevant and making such a big statement to a captive audience after inviting the country’s eminent and respected businessmen doesn’t carry the same weight that speaking at the relevant constitutional forums would have earned.” Asif said Naqvi had been on a “very powerful post” of the system for the past three years. “Had he wanted, he could have spoken about a change in the system or made progress on it during this time,” he said, moving to cite the DG ISPR’s remarks during Friday’s press briefing. The defence minister said the military’s spokesperson had referred to the NAP. “The implementation of one of its points, which is the armed forces’ responsibility, is being done by sacrificing lives. The implementation of the remaining 12 points is the interior ministry’s responsibility, but they have not been implemented. “Mohsin Naqvi sahib , begin the change in the system with the implementation of NAP; begin the change in the system with your ministry. Not just the respected business community, the entire nation is with you,” he added. Naqvi’s call for a reset of the system and creation of more administrative units has sparked a debate in the country, with the PPP referring the question to its top decision-making forum, the Sindh chief minister flatly rejecting it, Lahore’s lawyers terming it unconstitutional and Sindhi nationalist groups demanding the minister’s resignation. In the recent past, the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) — also an ally of the PML-N-led ruling coalition — has repeatedly demanded that Karachi be designated a province separate from Sindh. However, the PPP, which rules Sindh and is also an ally of the PML-N government at the Centre along with MQM-P, has strongly opposed the suggested move.

Second phase of AJK polls begins in Muzaffarabad division. The second phase of the Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) elections began on Sunday morning. Polling is being held in nine constituencies of Muzaffarabad division and all 12 refugee constituencies. Polling started at 8am and will continue without interruption till 5pm. Over 300 candidates are vying for nine Muzaffarabad seats and 12 seats for refugees settled in different regions. According to the AJK Election Commission, 207 candidates are in the fray for the nine constituencies in Muzaffarabad division, comprising five seats in Muzaffarabad district and two each in Neelum and Jhelum Valley districts. Another 137 candidates are contesting the 12 refugee constituencies, including six seats representing refugees from the Kashmir Valley and six from Jammu. A total of 809,621 voters are registered in Muzaffarabad division, while the 12 refugee constituencies have a combined electorate of 438,834. According to the commission, 1,483 polling stations have been established across Muzaffarabad division, of which 533 have been declared highly sensitive, 741 sensitive and 209 normal. Another 1,057 polling stations have been set up for the 12 refugee constituencies. Out of 12 refugee seats, seven seats are in Punjab, one seat is in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, one seat (Jammu-VI) is divided between Pun­jab, Islamabad, and Khyber Pakhtun­khwa, one seat is divided between Sindh and Balo­chistan (Valley-I), and one seat (Jammu-I) is shared among refugees living in Balochistan, Punjab, and Sindh. Valley-V seat is divided between Punjab and Islamabad. In Rawalpindi and Islamabad, about 27,000 registered male and female voters will elect lawmakers for LA-43 (Valley-IV), LA-44 (Valley-V), and LA-39 (Jammu-VI) seats. A total of 175 polling stations have been established, out of which 18 polling stations in Rawalpindi have been declared sensitive. A total of 34 candidates are in the fray. In Gujrat, almost 2,000 policemen will perform security duties at scores of polling stations for the LA-38 elections. The total number of polling stations in these districts is 115, with 75 in Gujrat, 24 in Wazirabad and 16 in Mandi Bahauddin. The total number of voters is 50,225 in the entire constituency. As many as 11 candidates are contesting this seat. In Sindh, officials said the elections will be conducted on LA-34 (Jammu-I) and LA-40 (Kashmir Valley-I) with polling stations established across Karachi and other districts of Sindh. In LA-34 (Jammu-I), a total of 17 candidates are contesting the election, which has 698 registered voters in Karachi’s seven districts and 477 voters in 13 other districts of Sindh. For LA-40 Kashmir (Valley-I), 11 candidates are in the race. The constituency has 4,200 registered voters in Karachi and 403 voters in 17 other districts of Sindh. In Balochistan, seven polling booths have been established across the province for the Kashmir Valley-I constituency, where 1,174 registered voters are expected to cast their ballots. Balochistan shares this seat with Sindh. For the Jammu-I constituency, six polling booths have been set up, with a total of 182 registered voters, including 85 men and 97 women, eligible to vote. Polling stations have been established for AJK refugee voters residing in Balochistan at various locations, including Quetta, Pishin, Qila Saifullah, Hub, Loralai, Sibi, Mastung, Zhob and Barkhan. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, 41 polling stations, mostly in Swat and Mansehra, have been set up for the LA-45 (Kashmir VI) seat. PPP says agents being prevented from sitting at polling station The PPP alleged that its polling agents were not being allowed to sit at polling stations in LA-34, calling on the Election Commission to intervene. Sardar Abdul Shakoor, the in-charge of the PPP’s AJK election cell, said the agents were being excluded due to them not being from the “local area”. He demanded that the Election Commission take notice of the incident and allow the PPP’s agents to perform their duties. In a separate statement in the morning, the party quoted Shakoor as claiming that no polling staff was present at any of the 196 polling stations in LA-27 in Muzaffarabad, adding that this raised the concern that there was a “deliberate” attempt to delay the polling. Similarly, the party alleged, polling staff had reached late at 71 polling stations of LA-28, due to which the polling process was facing delays. The PPP claimed that a similar situation was being witnessed at several polling stations of LA-30, where polling staff had not arrived on time. Regarding LA-31, the party said Shakoor had sent a written complaint to the Election Commission on behalf of its candidate contesting from the constituency, Chaudhry Latif Akbar. The party said the Election Commission was asked to take action over difficulties faced by voters due to the closure of the Rangla-Katker Road. The party said over 50 vehicles carrying voters were stuck due to the road’s closure. Allies’ rift continues to widen The PPP and the PML-N — coalition partners in the Centre — have been engaged in a war of words since the latter emerged victorious in Mirpur in the first phase of AJK elections. Despite multiple rounds of talks between the two parties in AJK, the tensions between the two allies over the results of the Mirpur elections did not subside, with leaders from both parties continuing to trade rigging allegations ahead of the second phase of the AJK elections. To defuse the tensions, senior leaders of both parties met multiple times in Azad Kashmir over the weekend to “explore a legal resolution” to the dispute. The latest round of talks followed two earlier meetings on Thursday and Friday. Another round was scheduled for Saturday afternoon, but could not be held as the PML-N leaders returned to Islamabad. A PML-N source told Dawn that discussions focused on the PPP’s allegations and its demand for re-polling in certain constituencies. “It was not planned or pre-planned rigging but isolated acts at places where supporters of one candidate enjoyed numerical dominance over their opponents. Such incidents have unfortunately been part of the territory’s polling atmosphere and have also been witnessed in previous elections,” the source quoted the PML-N leaders as telling their counterparts. According to the sources, the PPP initially raised objections to the results in four constituencies — Charhoi, Sehnsa and Nakyal in Kotli district, and Barnala in Bhimber district. However, it later withdrew its allegations regarding Sehnsa and Barnala. Saturday’s discussions centred on Charhoi, where PPP AJK president Chaudhry Yasin lost to PML-N’s Raja Riasat, and Nakyal, where PPP candidate Javed Iqbal Budhanvi was defeated by PML-N’s Raja Ayaz Ahmed. Meanwhile, the Sharif family also held discussions at Jati Umra. According to a statement issued by the PM’s Office, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif held consultations with his elder brother and PML-N chief Nawaz Sharif at Jati Umra to take stock of mounting political challenges, including the rift with the PPP over the AJK elections. A senior PML-N leader told Dawn that the party leadership had taken serious note of the PPP chairman’s increasingly combative rhetoric against the Sharif family over the AJK polls and his warning that the PPP could reconsider its support for the federal government if the remaining phases of the elections were manipulated in favour of the PML-N. Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz and Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar also attended the meeting.

South Korea records its highest-ever temperature of 42.5°C. South Korea registered on Sunday its highest temperature since records began more than a century ago, according to the state weather agency. The southeastern city of Yangsan saw the temperature reach 42.5 degrees Celsius at 1:26pm (9:26am PKT), the Korea Meteorological Administration said on its website. Yangsan has been the epicentre of the ongoing heatwave, where temperatures exceeded 40°C for a fifth consecutive day on Sunday. Much of South Korea has been placed under heat warnings, with many cities seeing temperatures climb into the high 30°C. More than 20 localities were on Sunday under emergency heatwave alerts, a new warning category introduced this year to better address rising temperatures. An emergency alert is issued when areas experiencing a heatwave are forecast to hit perceived temperatures of 38°C or an actual temperature of 39°C for one day. KMA data show the average annual number of heatwave days in the country has more than doubled to 19 over the past five years, from eight in the 1970s. A heatwave day is defined as one with a maximum temperature of at least 33°C, while a tropical night is one when the overnight low remains 25°C or above. Scientists warn that extreme weather events such as heatwaves are becoming more frequent and intense as a result of human-induced climate change.

Aurin the hero as gritty TNT pulls rug from under SMB in OT. Kim Aurin emerged as the unlikely hero in the endgame, burying two back-breaking triples as the undermanned but gritty TNT pulled the rug from under San Miguel, 93-89 in overtime in the PBA Season 50 Governors’ Cup at the Mall of Asia Arena on Saturday, Aug. 1. With the Tropang 5G missing most of its key players and needing someone to take over in the extra period, Aurin rose to the occasion and sparked a crucial 10-5 finishing kick to pick up its second-straight win and give head coach Chot Reyes a winning birthday celebration. Aurin was even fouled in his last three point make and while he missed the bonus free throw even had a crucial rebound to further fan the fiery TNT run. He finished with 22 points built on six triples to go with eight rebounds to step up in the absence of Calvin Oftana, Jayson Castro, RR Pogoy and Jordan Heading who are all out of commission due to their respective injuries. Import Rahlir Hollis-Jefferson also made a good account of himself in his first game back, finishing with 20 points, 13 rebounds and seven assists while Rey Nambatac also chipped in 21. Poy Erram was also solid in his first game back with 12 points as TNT improved to a 3-2 record while dragging SMB to a 4-2 slate. Leading by as many as 16 early on, TNT had to overcome a late explosion from George King who towed the Beermen to the overtime and even a 85-83 lead with 62 seconds left in the extra period. That, however, only set the table to the heroics of Aurin who actually played through a flu in the contest. King paced SMB with 35 points although he needed 28 attempts while making just nine to reach his output. He also shot 1-of-6 from the four-point territory. June Mar Fajardo added 14 points, 12 rebounds and two blocks while Marcio Lassiter and Don Trollano had 13 and 12 respectively.

LPA intensifies into Tropical Depression Luis. The low-pressure area (LPA) east of Infanta, Quezon intensified into Tropical Depression Luis on Saturday night, Aug. 1, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) reported. In a tropical cyclone update, the agency stated that the weather disturbance developed into Tropical Depression Luis at 8 p.m. “At 8:00 PM today (01 August 2026), the Low Pressure Area (LPA 07f) located east of Infanta, Quezon has developed into Tropical Depression LUIS,” it said. Per PAGASA, it will begin issuing Tropical Cyclone Bulletins for Luis starting at 11 p.m. The state weather bureau advised the public to continue monitoring official updates on “Luis.” Earlier this day, PAGASA said the LPA was unlikely to develop into a tropical cyclone within 24 hours. However, it intensified more quickly than previously anticipated and reached tropical depression status Saturday night.

Pro-education solon highlights another memorable quote from Marcos' SONA. President Marcos received standing ovations for his State of the Nation Address (SONA) remarks on scrapping systems loss charges and his nationalistic stand on the West Philippine Sea (WPS) issue. For Parañaque City 2nd district Rep. Brian Raymund Yamsuan, the Chief Executive made one more statement in his speech that deserved everyone's applause. “Tulad nga nang sinabi ng Pangulong Bongbong Marcos sa kanyang SONA, 'Edukasyon pa rin ang pangunahing nagtataguyod ng kakayahan,'" Yansuan said. (Like what President Bongbong Marcos said in his SONA, it is still education that is the primary factor in developing competence.) Incidentally, the House is just weeks away from tackling the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), wherein the education sector is expected to get the lion's share of the budget allocation. This scenario--along with the President's pronouncements--favored Yamsuan's advocacies, which included a bill that sought to develop a long-term plan to resolve the textbook shortage in public schools and "future-proof" learning materials for students. "This is why with the opening of Congress’ second regular session, we are hoping our measure could be taken up and swiftly acted upon as it will once and for all address the problem of the availability of textbooks in public schools, especially in areas outside Metro Manila and Luzon,” the solon said The second regular session of the 20th Congress began last July 27, the same day as Marcos' fifth SONA. According to a report by the Philippine Institute of Development Studies (PIDS) cited by the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), textbook production remains heavily concentrated in Luzon, with limited publishing capacity in the Visayas and Mindanao. To address this lack of publishing access outside Luzon, Yamsuan's House Bill (HB) No. 7868 mandates the printing of public elementary and secondary school textbooks at the regional or provincial level, whenever economically feasible. The bill also requires the Department of Education (DepEd) to phase out its elementary and secondary textbook publication and distribution functions within a three-year period and support the phasing in of private sector publishers to assume these tasks. Under HB No. 7868, the National Book Development Board (NBDB) will be given a broader role in the preparation and production of public school textbooks by mandating the DepEd to team up with it in jointly formulating a National Textbook and Learning Resources Plan. This Textbook Plan includes establishing policies, guidelines, and measures to ensure the availability of textbooks in all public schools as well as the review every five years of these learning materials to make them responsive to the needs of learners, Yamsuan said. He pointed out that while the DepEd has made commendable strides in bridging the textbooks-to-learner gap in public schools by allocating P19.5 billion for the production of textbooks this year and conducting early procurement activities, such initiatives need to be institutionalized under a comprehensive plan to ensure that learning materials in public schools meet industry standards and can readily address the educational needs of students. “Formulating a National Textbook and Learning Resources Plan will not only see to it that enough textbooks are available for our public school learners, it will also ensure that these and other learning materials are relevant and effective in educating future-ready Filipino learners,” the solon said. Malacañang is scheduled to submit the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP)--the precursor to the proposed national budget--to the House of Representatives on Aug. 14.

A question of history. FILLER As I was driving one of my aunts to lunch in Makati on a cloudy Tuesday morning, she told me about a video clip she had recently seen on YouTube. It was either a local quiz show or the quiz segment of a local noontime show—I honestly can't remember which. A question was asked about the Philippine flag: What do the eight rays of the sun symbolize? To the surprise of the host, and to the shock of my aunt, no one was able to answer. The contestants, she said, were about my age and older. (For those wondering, the answer is this: The eight rays of the sun represent the first eight provinces that took up arms against Spanish colonial rule—Manila, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Bulacan, Nueva Ecija, Tarlac, and Pampanga.) “Didn’t they learn that in school? We certainly did, back in the ’70s,” my aunt said. “Nakakalungkot naman, hindi na nila alam (How sad that they no longer know this).” And then our conversation moved to the latest SONA and what the President said about EPIRA. I definitely understand how my aunt felt. What she saw in that video was a reflection of a sad reality when it comes to Filipinos and Philippine history. There is a huge disconnect—or perhaps even a growing disinterest—in learning about the country’s history. For many, history is just another subject. For others, history is good for general knowledge quiz nights and for small talk. While these may be true about history and its more “practical” purposes, there is so much more to it. History is a nation’s identity. Without the past—as cliché as it may be—there is no present, nor can there be a better future. It is for this reason that an institution like the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) exists. Part of its mandate—aside from the identification, protection, and preservation of sites inherently connected to the country’s history and heritage—is to support studies of history on both the national and local levels. It does so in tandem with other government agencies through various activities that celebrate and promote appreciation for and the value of history. Currently, through initiatives such as histoEX (short for "history to experience"), the NHCP is encouraging research into local history—that is, the history of towns and provinces. Sadly, not many Filipinos are aware of the NHCP. Sadder still is the fact that this commission seems to be relegated as a second, maybe even third-class government agency, so to speak. This observation stems from an examination of the NHCP's budget, manpower, portfolio, and day-to-day functions. For starters, it runs some 28 museums all over the Philippines, all of which are free to the public. But that is a topic for another article. With August celebrated as Philippine History Month, it is good to reexamine the question of history and its role in the lives of Filipinos. Ironically, the easy access to information that the post-digital age has afforded us has also become one of our greatest enemies to true knowledge. Misinformation has become the norm, and history is one of its favorite subjects. A people that does not have a good grasp of its history can easily fall victim to the manipulation of historical facts. Nowadays, all it takes is a convincing video, often generated by artificial intelligence. So perhaps this Philippine History Month can be a little bit different from its previous iterations. History is not the study of dead people and their deeds, nor is it about knowing the dates of events that shaped our country’s past. History is also not about memorization; rather, it is about appreciation—for our nation’s story, in all its literal and figurative gore and glory. History is the answer to the “How did we get here?” question. Granted, there are official events organized not just by the NHCP but by other institutions invested in historical preservation. It is, however, not enough to simply just be aware of such activities or to participate in them. A true appreciation of Philippine history begins with a genuine curiosity to learn, and this is lived every day through the choices we make as a Filipino people. Contrary to how that other cliché goes, it is not history that repeats itself. It is societies and the people within them that fail to learn from history and therefore repeat the mistakes of yesteryears. For a nation to effectively move toward a better future, it needs to live fully in the present, which can only be done with a firm grasp of its past.

The social infrastructure of healthcare. HEARD IT THROUGH THE GRIPE-VINE True and efficient Universal Health Care has always been the pipe dream. While the Universal Health Care (UHC) Act, Republic Act No. 11223, was passed in 2019, with key features that included Automatic Enrollment, Primary Care Focus, Financial Protection, and Integrated Health Systems; the harsh reality of our fragmented healthcare infrastructure makes this vision more of a mirage. Besides the severe shortage of medical professionals, with many of the better qualified opting to work abroad; there are also underfunded facilities, plus bureaucratic roadblocks. Inadequate rural infrastructure makes access to basic diagnostics a limited scenario in the countryside, with no acceptable basic standard for LGUs across the board. Some will be super-efficient and impressive, while others woefully lacking in resources. In fairness, there has been a lot of progress since 2019, but we still face an uphill struggle; a battle that’s being waged daily. As it’s not like we can say stop getting sick, contracting lethal diseases, or dying; while we first fix and upgrade the system. For a typical Thai citizen, their Universal Health Care Coverage Scheme, has their out of pocket (OOP) medical expenses representing around 10 percent of total health expenditures (Data Bank/The World Bank). Contrast that to here in the Philippines, where the average Filipino citizen has to directly shoulder around 41.2 percent of their health care expenditures (Philippine Statistics Authority). This despite the National Insurance and Government programs that exist. So you can immediately see how there’s so much room for improvement. So that’s why I’m always ready to feature and support the private companies who are ready to take on the responsibility, and be among the leading healthcare providers in this nation. The Healthway Medical Network (HMN) is dedicated to delivering exceptional care and improving the lives of Filipinos. A wholly-owned subsidiary of AC Health, the healthcare arm of the Ayala Corporation; HMN operates via integrating four major business units - Healthway Multi-Specialty Clinics, Healthway QualiMed Hospitals, the Healthway FEU-NRMF Medical Center, and the Healthway Cancer Care Hospital. The Cancer Care Hospital I’ve written about extensively; being witness to its’ rise in Arca South, and its’ inauguration in November, 2023. The Healthway Medical Network represents more than 2,000 physicians, and 2,500 allied health professionals. From prevention to rehabilitation, HMN prides itself on its personalized humancentric care, and how it is supported by advancing health technology. It also promotes PhilHealth alignment, to help make care accessible, and medication affordable — supporting UHC mandates. Just last month, in July, AC Health opened the Healthway Multi-Specialty Center at One Ayala, and it now stands as their flagship outpatient facility in Makati. It used to exist at Greenbelt; but in the interest of access ability, it is now housed in a building that’s also one of Metro Manila’s busiest transport hubs. As Paolo Borromeo, AC Health CEO was ready to explain, “By bringing comprehensive, specialist-led care closer to where Filipinos commute every day, we are making it easier to prioritize health without disrupting work, family, or daily responsibilities. From consultations and diagnostics to ambulatory procedures, dialysis, women’s health services, and seamless access to pharmacy care through St. Joseph Drug, Powered by Sugi, every element of this center was designed around the patient experience.” Elevating and upgrading the patient experience is what this Center prioritizes. And because of its’ strategic location at Level 4 of the One Ayala Mall, there’s a diverse range of offerings for Food while one waits for results; and even for those accompanying the patient, the Mall offers endless possibilities of how to spend one’s waiting time. As for the Center itself, before it was opened to the assembled media, Dra. Michelle Anievas had overheard how I had to leave even before the lunch would be served, and offered to tour me around. And can I say right here that I was very impressed with how much they packed into the Center, given that it’s in the mall, and not a standalone hospital or medical facility. The Dialysis Center has twelve stations, and is equipped with the latest dialysis machines. There is an ambulatory surgery center for outpatient procedures, and diagnostics and imaging services are found in another of the rooms. Executive check-ups and rehabilitation facilities are also offered here – and as I live across Ayala Avenue, I loved them saying that my next PSAT (Prostate Specific Antigen Test) could be done there. After my brush with Prostate Cancer in 2021, my urologist requires I submit PSAT results every six months. A dedicated Women’s Center offers Mammograms, OB and Breast Ultrasound. And as the media press con stressed, the big idea was to integrate within the network. So that an oncologist could see patients at One Ayala, then recommend they transfer to Arca South. Healthway is literally showing the way, and playing its role, in moving us closer to true Universal Health Care.

Government service as a vocation: Lessons in humility, perseverance. ENDEAVOR Today, I take a respite from writing about current events and issues. Instead, I will reflect on government service as a vocation. After more than a decade of working in private organizations – in a bank, a holding company, and a transportation company – I decided to avail myself of opportunities to serve in government, thanks to a work leave privilege extended by my employer and alma mater, the Asian Institute of Management. I served briefly in the Department of Agrarian Reform, upon the invitation of then Secretary Miriam Defensor Santiago, then opted to transfer to the Department of Transportation and Communications (DOTC) when she left office. Moreover, I was privileged to serve in the Office of the President twice: first, under President Corazon C. Aquino, then with her son, President Benigno S. Aquino III. In all my stints in public service, writing and public speaking were important daily responsibilities. Dealing with different stakeholders involved being able to respond to their needs and wants — and this could be achieved only by taking time to understand their situation. Let me focus on my service with President Noynoy Aquino, as this was my longest stint, having served for the entire duration of his six-year term of office from 2010 to 2016. The work of the President – and the rest of government – is chronicled daily by the mass media. We relied heavily on the working press to convey the rationale to convey the rationale for salient government policies and programs. With the emergence of digital technology, mass communication has changed tremendously. Legacy media – as exemplified by the printed newspaper and live radio broadcasting – has been relegated to the background. People now rely on their cellular phones and other digital devices, more than reading books or tuning in to their erstwhile favorite radio or TV channels. Separating the proverbial chaff from grain, and discerning what’s factually true from what is being peddled as fake news is not an easy chore. In this day and age, peddling fake news has become part of the tool kit of traditional politicians. Hence, my fellow Baby Boomers and I are now compelled to seek guidance from tech-savvy children and grandchildren to help us sort things out. How are government officials today helped – or harmed – by the power of digital media? In the past, when legacy media ruled the day, the government of the day had to stay focused and ensure consistency of its messaging. Presently, the imperative is the same, with the added burden of needing strong political will to overcome the vagaries of negativism being spread by the denizens of disinformation and fake news. Even If a public servant takes the high ground and avows fidelity to truth, reason and justice, such a noble posture would not provide adequate safety or comfort from the tribulations inflicted by their adversaries. Let me cite a concrete example. Long after former President Aquino stepped down in 2016, the justice department ordered investigations and filed charges against Aquino and former health officials for allegedly rushing the procurement and rolling out the Dengvaxia vaccine to hundreds of thousands of schoolchildren. The former president, in his defense, said that “…there has been no categorical finding by medical experts that the dengue vaccine has directly caused the deaths of vaccinated children. At the time of the funding approval, there was no evidence adduced by the experts that the vaccine was not safe and effective.” Affirming that the Dengvaxia program underwent proper procurement process, he pointed out further: “There has not been any definitive finding by any court, tribunal or fact-finding body as to whether the deaths suffered were directly attributable to the vaccine,” he noted. Aquino said the program was above board, and effectively addressed the increasing threat of the disease. In 2023, two years after former President Aquino’s death, the Supreme Court dismissed a petition filed in 2017 by the women’s group Gabriela and more than 70 children who sought to compel the government to address the health risks posed by the controversial Dengvaxia dengue vaccine. The High Court said that it did not find “any serious or systematic inability” of respondents in the performance of their duties. It said in its ruling: “Considering that these are agencies possessing the technical knowledge and specialization in their fields, the judgments of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the DOH are given significant weight and should not be impulsively disturbed.” It noted further that when the vaccine was approved by the FDA, “there (was) a reasonable presumption that the approval is based on science and the subsequent recommendation by the DOH enjoys a presumption of constitutionality.” Such are the vagaries and downsides of serving in government. Yet, when I look back and reflect, I maintain that it was a singular opportunity to have worked and served with President Noynoy Aquino. Indeed, it was a fitting capstone to my several stints in government service that taught me valuable lessons in perseverance, resilience and humility. Comments may be sent to sonnycoloma@gmail.com

The feeding of the five thousand. REFLECTIONS TODAY First Reading • Is 55:1-3 Thus says the Lord: All you who are thirsty, come to the water! You who have no money, come, receive grain and eat; come, without paying and without cost, drink wine and milk! Why spend your money for what is not bread; your wages for what fails to satisfy? Heed me, and you shall eat well, you shall delight in rich fare. Come to me heedfully, listen, that you may have life. I will renew with you the everlasting covenant,/ the benefits assured to David. Responsorial Psalm • Ps 145 “The hand of the Lord feeds us; he answers all our needs.” Second Reading • Rom 8:35, 37-39 Brothers and sisters: What will separate us from the love of Christ? Will anguish, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword? No, in all these things we conquer overwhelmingly through him who loved us. For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor present things, nor future things, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Gospel • Mt 14:13-21 When Jesus heard of the death of John the Baptist, he withdrew in a boat to a deserted place by himself. The crowds heard of this and followed him on foot from their towns. When he disembarked and saw the vast crowd, his heart was moved with pity for them, and he cured their sick. When it was evening, the disciples approached him and said, “This is a deserted place and it is already late; dismiss the crowds so that they can go to the villages and buy food for themselves.” Jesus said to them, “There is no need for them to go away; give them some food yourselves.” But they said to him, “Five loaves and two fish are all we have here.” Then he said, “Bring them here to me,” and he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass. Taking the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he said the blessing, broke the loaves, and gave them to the disciples, who in turn gave them to the crowds. They all ate and were satisfied, and they picked up the fragments left over—twelve wicker baskets full. Those who ate were about five thousand men, not counting women and children. A little sacrifice can bring overflowing abundance. THROUGH UNTRUE In today's Gospel, Jesus asks His disciples to feed the tired and hungry crowd that had been following Him. Their response, however, sounds discouraging: “Five loaves and two fish are all we have here” (Mt. 14:17). They forget that Jesus can turn what seems insufficient into overflowing abundance. If they willingly sacrifice the little that they have, a hundredfold reward awaits them. Many people, however, understand the “hundredfold reward” in a purely transactional or mathematical way. They imagine that if they give two hundred pesos to the poor, God will reward them with twenty thousand pesos in return. Such thinking reduces God to a lottery machine and strips sacrifice of its deepest meaning. The reward Jesus promises is far greater than material prosperity. Every time we give up something for God, we enlarge our capacity to enjoy a loving relationship with Him whose love and generosity is boundless. Every act of self-denial reminds us that no created thing deserves our absolute attachment. Gradually, we come to discover that if God is all we have, then God is all we need. Imagine a child walking with his father across a crowded street. The child owns nothing and carries no money in his pocket. Yet he feels that he lacks nothing because he is holding the hand of the one who loves and provides for him. Our security likewise comes from the certainty that God never lets go of our hand in moments of need. Many of us are allergic to sacrifices because we think that what we give up will be lost forever. What if we need it someday? Also, we fear that the time, money, or effort we invested in acquiring it will be wasted. Constantly calculating these trade-offs can leave us emotionally drained and reluctant to let go. But this is precisely why we need to examine and continually rearrange our priorities. We must ask ourselves uncomfortable but necessary questions: What truly matters in my life? Why do I always feel that I do not have enough? Why do I seek security in buying and hoarding things even when I already have so much? In a world where almost everything we desire can be purchased online and delivered to our doorstep within days or hours, it is easy to become trapped in a cycle of endless shopping, buying, and hoarding. Little by little, the things we acquire begin to crowd out the things that matter most: our peace of mind, our self-respect, our contentment, and, above all, our relationship with God, our family, and our friends. Possessions make wonderful servants but terrible masters. The more we accumulate without learning to let go, the more our possessions tyrannize us, until we believe that our happiness depends on having more. Eventually, we lose the freedom to live peacefully because we become burdened by the constant fear of losing what we own. Today's Gospel teaches us that sacrifice becomes easier when it is inspired by love. Giving up something for someone we love does not feel like a loss but a privilege. A mother gladly sacrifices sleep to care for her sick child. A husband or wife willingly sets aside personal comfort for the good of the family. True friends make sacrifices without keeping score because a friend’s joy becomes their own. God Himself is the supreme example of sacrificial love. As the Gospel proclaims, “For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that whoever believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life” (Jn. 3:16). St. Thomas Aquinas explains that Christ did not die on the cross because our sins were simply too great to forgive. Rather, His death reveals the immeasurable breadth, length, height, and depth of God's love for us. Every little sacrifice made for God enlarges our freedom and deepens our gratitude for God’s abundant blessings. Today, ask yourself: “God has given me so much. What have I given up for Him lately?”

Embrace YAKAP as preventive healthcare. The true measure of a healthcare program is not how much it promises but how many lives it actually improves. The Yaman ng Kalusugan Program (YAKAP), PhilHealth's expanded primary healthcare initiative, has the potential to transform preventive healthcare. Yet despite growing enrollment, its utilization remains strikingly low. Millions of Filipinos have signed up, but only a small fraction have sought consultations and availed themselves of its benefits. That disconnect is a public health concern the country can no longer afford to ignore. YAKAP represents a fundamental shift from treating illness to preventing it. Through free medical consultations, laboratory tests, and outpatient medicines under the complementary PhilHealth GAMOT package, members may receive up to ₱20,000 worth of essential medicines annually from more than 2,000 accredited providers. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s pledge to expand coverage to include blood tests and medicines for kidney, liver, thyroid diseases, and hepatitis B is a welcome step toward strengthening primary healthcare. But no expansion will succeed if Filipinos remain passive beneficiaries instead of active participants. Too many people still visit health facilities only after symptoms become unbearable, when treatment is often more difficult and expensive. Preventive healthcare demands a different mindset. Regular consultations can detect hypertension before it triggers a stroke, diabetes before it damages vital organs, or liver disease before complications become irreversible. Early diagnosis saves lives, preserves productivity, and reduces the financial burden on families and the healthcare system alike. Every unused YAKAP benefit is a missed opportunity to prevent suffering. Filipinos should therefore move beyond merely enrolling in the program. They should register with an accredited YAKAP provider, keep their PhilHealth records updated, schedule routine medical consultations even when they feel healthy, complete recommended laboratory examinations, obtain prescribed medicines through accredited providers, and faithfully return for follow-up care. Preventive healthcare is effective only when people consistently use it. The government, for its part, must match expanded benefits with efficient implementation. The success of YAKAP depends on accessible facilities, sufficient healthcare professionals, uninterrupted medicine supplies, reliable laboratory services, and digital systems that simplify registration, appointments, and benefit tracking. Public information campaigns should be sustained nationwide, especially in underserved communities where many remain unaware of the program or uncertain about how to access it. Universal healthcare cannot be achieved if awareness remains selective and access uneven. The private sector, particularly accredited YAKAP providers, must become indispensable partners in making preventive healthcare truly work. Beyond meeting accreditation standards, healthcare providers should deliver patient-centered care by reducing waiting times, maintaining adequate medicine inventories, improving patient education, extending clinic hours where feasible, and using digital reminders to encourage regular consultations. Employers, schools, civil society organizations, and local governments can likewise help promote enrollment and routine health screening, transforming preventive care into a community norm rather than an individual choice. Ultimately, healthcare is a shared responsibility. The government can build the system, healthcare institutions can deliver quality services, and private partners can broaden access. But every Filipino must choose to invest in personal well-being by seeking timely medical advice, taking prescribed medicines properly, embracing healthy habits, exercising regularly, eating nutritious food, avoiding tobacco and excessive alcohol, and recognizing that prevention is always better than cure. Rather than considering YAKAP as an expense incurred during illness, it must instead be viewed as an opportunity to redefine how the nation values health and an investment for one’s wellbeing. President Marcos’ vision of expanded preventive healthcare can become a lasting national achievement only if the government fulfills its commitments, healthcare providers continuously raise service standards, and Filipinos make full use of a program designed not merely to treat disease, but to prevent it before it begins.

Eala stuns Osaka, marches into first WTA 500 final. Alex Eala added another marquee scalp to her growing list of giant-killing feats, stunning former world No. 1 and four-time Grand Slam champion Naomi Osaka, 6-4, 6-2, to storm into the finals of the Mubadala DC Open in Washington D.C. on Sunday, Aug. 2 (Philippine time). The world No. 28 Filipina showcased her poise and grit against the hard-hitting, third-seeded Osaka, digging deep in a tough contest to reach her first-ever WTA 500 championship match. It was also Eala’s second career final following her runner-up finish at the WTA 125 Eastbourne last year. Awaiting Eala in the final is top seed and world No. 3 Jessica Pegula, who earlier dispatched fourth pick Diana Shnaider, 7-5, 6-4. “I think I played really well and I had a great mentality and I stayed locked in till the end,” said Eala. “She definitely has aura and she definitely has power, I can tell you… So it’s really a great experience to share the court with her and I’m really happy that I was able to produce that level against her,” she added. Eala and Osaka matched each other shot for shot in the opening set, exchanging service breaks in the third and fourth games before settling into a string of holds that kept the score tied at 4-all. But consecutive unforced errors from Osaka proved costly, allowing Eala to break serve and grab a pivotal 5-4 lead. Riding the momentum, Eala comfortably held the next game to seal the first set in her favor, then stormed to a 2-0 lead in the second set to stay in complete control. A decisive break in the seventh game all but sealed Osaka's fate as the Filipina wrapped up the stunning victory in one hour and 16 minutes.

The tournament gathered 64 elite players offering a total pot of $200,000 (around P12.3 million) with $55,000 (around P3.3 million) to the winner.

China warns of ‘resolute’ response over Philippine baselines around Bajo de Masinloc. China has warned that it would "respond resolutely" if the Philippines continues what Beijing described as acts of infringement or provocation around Bajo de Masinloc, as it rejected Manila's delimitation of territorial sea baselines around the disputed shoal. In a statement posted on the Chinese Embassy in Manila’s Facebook page, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs urged the Philippines to respect what Beijing claims as its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests over Huangyan Dao, its name for Bajo de Masinloc, also known internationally as Scarborough Shoal. "China urges the Philippines to earnestly respect China’s territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests, and refrain from any act of infringement or provocation in Huangyan Dao," the ministry said. "Otherwise, China will respond resolutely," it added. Beijing accused Manila of repeatedly engaging in what it called provocations around the shoal and of using maritime disputes between the two countries to heighten tensions in the South China Sea. "For some time, the Philippines has been frequently making provocations in the waters of Huangyan Dao and hyping the maritime issues between China and the Philippines," the Chinese Foreign Ministry said, claiming that such actions "heighten maritime tensions, and undermine peace and stability in the South China Sea." China rejects PH baselines China also rejected the Philippines' delimitation of what Manila considers the territorial sea baselines around Bajo de Masinloc, describing the move as a violation of Chinese sovereignty and international law. "The Philippines’ delimitation of the so-called ‘baselines of the territorial sea’ of China’s territory of Huangyan Dao (Huangyan Island) is a grave infringement upon China’s territorial sovereignty and a serious violation of international law including the United Nations Charter and the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)," the ministry said. "It is illegal, null and void. China firmly rejects and will never accept it," it added. Beijing maintained that the shoal is China's "inherent territory" and claimed "indisputable sovereignty" over it and its adjacent waters, arguing that the feature was never included in Philippine territory as defined by international treaties. Beijing hits Maritime Zones Act, arbitral ruling China likewise assailed the Philippines' Maritime Zones Act, accusing Manila of using domestic legislation to reinforce the landmark 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award and include Bajo de Masinloc and features in the Spratly Islands within Philippine maritime zones. Beijing claimed that the law "severely violates China's territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests in the South China Sea," insisting that its claims would not be affected by Philippine legislation. China also renewed its rejection of the 2016 Arbitral Award, maintaining that the Philippines' initiation of arbitration violated international law, previous bilateral agreements, and the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea. "The so-called ‘award’ is illegal, null and void, and has no binding force,” the Chinese Foreign Ministry said. “China neither accepts nor recognizes the ‘award,’ and opposes and will never accept any claim or action based on it," it added. The 2016 tribunal, however, ruled that there was no legal basis for China's sweeping claims to historic rights within its so-called "nine-dash line" under UNCLOS, while also making findings concerning the maritime entitlements of features in the South China Sea. PH turns to international law Beijing's latest warning comes as the Philippines continues to invoke UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award in asserting its maritime entitlements in the West Philippine Sea. The Philippines recently formally presented before the United Nations Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf (CLCS) its partial submission concerning the country's entitlement to an extended continental shelf in the West Philippine Sea covering the West Palawan Region. During the presentation at the United Nations Headquarters, the Philippine delegation asked the Commission to consider relevant decisions of tribunals constituted under UNCLOS, including the 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award, which determined maritime entitlements of littoral states in the South China Sea. The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said the submission demonstrates the Philippines' commitment to the UN Charter and UNCLOS and reflects the country's reliance on a rules-based order to promote a peaceful South China Sea, sustain Filipino livelihoods, foster trade, protect marine biodiversity, and strengthen cooperation among coastal states. The submission was prepared over 15 years by the Extended Continental Shelf Technical Working Group led by the National Mapping and Resource Information Authority, with the Philippine delegation to the CLCS headed by Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the United Nations Enrique A. Manalo. Marcos: PH will uphold arbitral award President Marcos also recently vowed that the government would continue defending the country's landmark arbitral victory through peaceful and legal means, using his fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA) to declare that the Philippines would not abandon the 2016 ruling. "This is not a claim that we advance alone, nor one that we will abandon," he said. "Your government will do all that is necessary to continue upholding this Award, utilizing every peaceful and legal means available to the Republic against any attempt, foreign or domestic, to undermine this achievement," he added. The President likewise paid tribute to the Armed Forces of the Philippines, the Philippine Coast Guard, and Filipino fisherfolk who continue to operate in the West Philippine Sea despite the risks they face, saying their presence gives life to the "letter and spirit" of the arbitral ruling. Marcos also called for national unity in defending Philippine sovereignty amid continuing security challenges. "We are not greedy. We are not racists. We are not liars. We are respectful, and we are dignified. We are Filipinos, and we do not yield," he said.

All 10 climbers swept away in avalanche in Pakistan are confirmed dead. ISLAMABAD (AP) — Renowned British-Nepali climber Nirmal Purja and nine other climbers swept away by an avalanche in Pakistan are confirmed to have died, and search teams are trying to recover their bodies, Purja's expedition company said Saturday. "The world has lost one of mountaineering's greatest climbers," the company, Elite Exped, said in a statement. It stressed that it mourned all the lives lost, adding: "No words can ease the pain of this unimaginable loss." The 10-member expedition was swept away by an avalanche Thursday on Pakistan's Broad Peak. Rescuers found four bodies and recovered three of them Friday in harsh weather that hampered flights by search and rescue helicopters. Rescuers backed by military helicopters had resumed a search earlier on Saturday for the others. "The loss of these courageous climbers, who came from different nations united by their passion for the mountains, is an immeasurable loss to the global mountaineering fraternity," said Irfan Arshad Khan, the president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan. Khan paid tribute to the military and civilian rescuers and sherpas who took part in the search mission. "The mountains inspire us with their beauty, but they also remind us of the immense risks faced by those who venture into the high Himalaya and Karakoram," he said.
